scenario: AITA for my gf and I keeping our income low to apply for lower income housing. | Ok so this is weird. My girlfriend and I have been looking to move in together so we’ve been searching for apartments. My parents recently onformed me that they’d be moving to Phoenix, AZ in August so I would need to find my own place. A lot of the apartments were too expensive for our budget but we found 1 that we’re happy with. The complex was very nice and the lost cost we were told was 890/mo for 1 bed/1 bath. We were also informed of this application where if you and whoever are living in the apartment are making less than 32000 collectively a year then you apply for the “bond program” (I think it was called) that let’s you live in their studio apartments for less rent (about 550 a month not including utilities) We asked about the availability of the apartment and they told us that there are a lot available right now so it’s not like people are scrambling to get in. My gf has been looking for a new job and would like to switch to full time when she finishes college. I told her that she should wait until we apply and get the verification that we apply for the program to actually go full time and she agreed. We wouldn’t apply until July. (She’s not struggling for cash or anything and i would help out if that ever were the case, this would strictly be to save money in the long run). We also started trying to attack our debts together and would be basically living like poor people for the foreseeable future until we were out of debt. So this program would give us a head start. After the leasing period, if your income rises above 32000 a year you’d be asked to move into the normal studio (which is the same size and specs as the bond program one). We cooould afford to live in the normal apartments comfortably but it would take longer to pay off our debts. AITA?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether it's right or wrong for me and my girlfriend to keep our income low so we can apply for lower-income housing. Let me break this down step by step. First, we're looking to move in together, and my parents are moving to Phoenix, so I need to find my own place. We found an apartment complex that's nice, and the rent is $890 a month for a 1-bedroom. But there's this bond program where if our combined income is less than $32,000 a year, we can get a lower rent of about $550 a month. That's a significant saving. We asked about availability, and they said there are a lot of apartments available right now, so it's not like people are scrambling to get in. My girlfriend is looking for a new job and wants to switch to full-time after she finishes college. I told her to wait until we apply and get verified for the program before going full-time, and she agreed. We won't apply until July. She's not struggling for cash, and I would help out if needed, but this is strictly to save money in the long run. We're also trying to pay off our debt, so we'll be living like poor people for the foreseeable future until we're out of debt. This program would give us a head start. After the leasing period, if our income rises above $32,000 a year, we'd have to move into the normal studio apartment, which is the same size and specs as the bond program one. We could afford the normal apartments comfortably, but it would take longer to pay off our debts. So, is it right or wrong to keep our income low to apply for this program? I'm not sure. On one hand, it's a smart financial move to save money and pay off debt faster. On the other hand, is it ethical to underreport our income or not seek higher-paying jobs just to qualify for lower rent? I also wonder about the long-term implications. If we keep our income low now, will it affect our ability to get better jobs or advance in our careers? And what happens if our income does go above $32,000? We'd have to move, which could disrupt our plans. Another thing to consider is whether this program is intended for people who genuinely need lower-income housing. If we're doing this just to save money, are we taking advantage of a system meant for those in greater need? There's also the aspect of honesty. If we're applying for the program, do we need to disclose our financial situation accurately? Could there be consequences if we're found to have misrepresented our income? I'm also thinking about the practical side. How easy is it to keep our income low? If my girlfriend gets a full-time job, will that push our combined income over the limit? And how does that affect our application? Overall, I'm torn between making a smart financial decision and doing what's ethically right. I need to weigh the benefits of saving money and paying off debt against the potential ethical issues and long-term consequences of keeping our income low to qualify for the program.
